purpose: Bedaquiline is used to treat a serious type of tuberculosis (TB) called multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), which is TB that does not respond to the usual TB medicines. It is always used together with other TB medicines, never alone. It helps people who have run out of other effective treatment options.
how_it_works: TB bacteria need a special energy-making 'engine' inside them to survive and multiply. Bedaquiline works by blocking that engine — called ATP synthase — so the bacteria cannot produce the energy they need to live. Without energy, the bacteria die off, helping your body fight the infection. It targets TB bacteria in a unique way that most other antibiotics do not.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, joint pain, headache, chest pain, and feeling tired. Some people also notice dizziness or coughing. Most of these side effects are manageable, but let your doctor or pharmacist know if they bother you.
warnings: Bedaquiline can cause a serious change in your heart rhythm called QT prolongation, which can be dangerous or even life-threatening. Your doctor will monitor your heart with regular EKGs while you are on this medicine. Do not take it with certain other medicines that also affect heart rhythm without telling your doctor. It can also affect your liver, so avoid alcohol and report any yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain right away. This medicine should not be used during pregnancy unless absolutely necessary.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 400 mg (four 100 mg tablets) taken by mouth once a day for the first 2 weeks, and then 200 mg three times a week for the next 22 weeks — for a total of 24 weeks of treatment. Always take it with food, as this helps your body absorb the medicine much better. Never skip doses, and do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
